Part Three · Administration and Configuration

Administration and Configuration

◆

Creating tenants, granting access, and configuring an installation that can be rebuilt from documentation.

8.1 Creating laundries

A laundry is a tenant. Creating one is a platform operation performed by a PLATFORM_ADMIN, because it establishes the boundary inside which every later record will live. Laundry administrators cannot create tenants; they administer the one they belong to.

Table 50 — What a new laundry requires
ElementPurpose
Name and short codeDisplay name and a stable short reference used on documents
StatusActive or suspended; a suspended tenant can sign in to read but not to write
Currency and tax configurationApplied to every bill raised in the tenant
First administratorAn existing user granted ADMIN membership, or a new user created for the purpose

Procedure — creating a laundry

8 · Administration and ConfigurationLoveLaundry — System Manual
  1. Sign in as a platform administrator and open the tenant administration screen.
  2. Create the laundry: name, short code, currency and tax rate. Check the tax rate against the jurisdiction before saving — changing it later does not alter issued bills.
  3. Create or select the first administrator's user account.
  4. Add a membership linking that user to the new laundry with the ADMIN role.
  5. Sign in as that administrator in a private window and confirm that the tenant name appears and that an empty dashboard loads.
  6. Record the creation in the platform change log with the operator and the time.
Warning

Do not reuse a short code, even for a closed laundry. Short codes appear on printed documents and in exports; a reused code makes two businesses' history indistinguishable.

8.2 · Users and memberships

Users and memberships

The platform separates a person from their access. A user is an identity — an email, a password hash, a display name. A membership is that identity's link to one laundry, carrying a role. One person may hold memberships in several laundries and one role in each.

Table 51 — Role assignment guidance
RoleGive it toDo not give it to
ADMINThe owner and at most one deputyEvery manager, by default
MANAGERSupervisors who close days and handle moneyCounter assistants
STAFFOperational data entryAnyone who approves refunds
LINEN_SUPERVISORThe person accountable for linen lossSeasonal staff without handover responsibility
HOUSEKEEPERScanning and finishing staffAnyone who prints tags or retires items

Procedure — adding a user to a laundry

  1. Open Users and select Add user.
  2. Enter the person's own email address. Shared mailboxes and role-based addresses make the audit trail useless.
  3. Set an initial password and require a change at first sign-in.
  4. Add the membership: choose the laundry (fixed to your own tenant if you are not a platform administrator) and the role.
  5. Ask the user to sign in while you are present, so that a mistyped address is discovered immediately.

Removing access

◆82◆
8 · Administration and ConfigurationLoveLaundry — System Manual

Removing someone's access means removing the membership or disabling the user, never deleting history. A deleted user leaves records attributed to nobody, which is exactly the situation an audit cannot tolerate. Disabling the user prevents new sign-ins; existing tokens remain valid until they expire, so a departure that requires immediate certainty also requires a signing-key rotation or a documented acceptance of the residual window.

Note

Changing a role takes effect at the next sign-in, because capabilities are carried in the token. If a change must apply immediately, disable the user and re-enable them so that a fresh token is issued.

8.3 · Hotel client accounts and roles

Hotel client accounts and roles

Hotel accounts live in a separate collection from staff users, and they are created by the laundry that serves the hotel. The account binds an email and password to exactly one client_name within the laundry, which is the whole of its authority.

Table 52 — Client account record
FieldMeaning
EmailSign-in identity for the hotel user
Password hashSalted hash; never displayed or exported
laundry_idThe tenant whose records the account may read
client_nameThe one hotel whose records are visible
RoleHOTEL_ADMIN or HOTEL_MANAGER
StatusActive or disabled

Procedure — creating a hotel account

  1. Confirm the exact client_name spelling used on the hotel's gate passes and bills. A variant spelling creates an account that sees nothing.
  2. Create the client account with the hotel's contact email and a role.
  3. Communicate the credentials through a channel the hotel controls; never send a password in the same message as the sign-in address.
  4. Ask the hotel to sign in and confirm they can see their own passes and invoices.
  5. Record the creation and the operator in the change log.

Enabling and disabling accounts

A client account is disabled when a property changes management, when a member of staff leaves, or when credentials are suspected compromised. Disabling is immediate for new sign-ins and is recorded with the operator and reason. The endpoints are GET /client/auth/status for the account's own state, GET|POST /clients for listing and creating accounts, and PATCH /clients/{id}/status for changing an account's state.

◆83◆
8 · Administration and ConfigurationLoveLaundry — System Manual
Warning

Never create a client account with a staff role, and never add a client account to a membership. The two identity systems are separate so that a hotel token can never satisfy a staff authorisation check.

8.4 · Environment variables

Environment variables

Configuration is supplied through the environment. Nothing that differs between installations is compiled into the code, and nothing secret is committed to the repository. The table lists the variables an operator must set; names follow the service that reads them.

Table 53 — Required configuration
VariableRead byPurpose
MONGO_URIAll servicesDatabase connection string, with TLS and the service's own credential
DB_NAMEPer serviceThe database the service owns (user_db, operations, accounting)
JWT_SIGNING_KEYuser-serviceSigns staff tokens; rotated on the schedule in 13.4
JWT_VERIFY_KEYSAll servicesKey set used to verify tokens, including the next key during rotation
JWT_TTL_STAFF / JWT_TTL_CLIENTuser-serviceToken lifetimes: 24 hours and 12 hours
KEK_ID / KEK_MATERIALbill_service, user-serviceKey-encryption key reference and material for envelope encryption
SEARCH_KEYbill_serviceHMAC key for deterministic search tokens
CORS_ORIGINSAll servicesExact front-end origins permitted to call the API
LOG_LEVELAll servicesVerbosity; production defaults to structured informational logging
RATE_LIMIT_*Proxy and servicesThresholds per class, as described in 3.5

Front-end configuration

Each React application reads build-time variables prefixed VITE_. Only public values belong there — service base URLs, environment name, feature flags — because everything so prefixed is embedded in the bundle and readable by anyone with a browser. A secret placed in a VITE_ variable is published, not configured.

VITE_API_BASE=/api
VITE_ENV=production
VITE_ENABLE_AI_ASSIST=true
Warning

Changing a signing key or a KEK is not a routine configuration edit. Follow the rotation procedures in 3.6; an unplanned change invalidates every session or makes encrypted fields unreadable.

8.5 · Deployment steps

Deployment steps

A deployment is a build, a configuration check, a service restart and a smoke test — in that order. The steps below assume a single application host behind a reverse proxy, as described in 2.9.

◆84◆
8 · Administration and ConfigurationLoveLaundry — System Manual

Procedure — deploying a release

  1. Build the four front-end bundles from the tagged commit. Record the commit hash in the change log.
  2. Confirm the environment file contains every required variable, and that no secret is present in a VITE_ variable.
  3. Apply any database index changes for the release. Index creation is online in MongoDB and must precede the code that depends on it.
  4. Stop and restart each service in dependency order: user-service, bill_service, then the supporting services.
  5. Verify health: sign in as a staff user, load the dashboard, open a gate pass, and confirm the hotel portal rejects a staff token.
  6. Publish the new static bundles. Because filenames are hashed, the old bundles remain valid until the proxy switch.
  7. Watch the error log for five minutes, then declare the release complete — or roll back by restoring the previous bundle and the previous service version.
Table 54 — Rollback decision points
SymptomRollback?Note
Sign-in failing for everyoneYes, immediatelyUsually a key or configuration mismatch
One screen erroringNoFix forward; rollback does not restore data written since
Bills wrong after releaseYes, and stop writesPreserve the database state before any further action
Slow but functionalNoInvestigate before rolling back a working system
Warning

Never deploy on a Friday afternoon or immediately before a day close. A release that fails at close leaves the business unable to bill, and the person who can fix it is least available.

◆85◆
9

Part Three · Disaster Management

Disaster Management

◆

What can go wrong, how bad it would be, and who does what in the first hour.

9.1 Framework and risk method

Disaster management here means the decisions made before an incident, so that during one nobody has to invent a process. The framework has four parts: a risk register that names and ranks the threats, a severity matrix that determines the response, a runbook that sequences the first hour, and a review that turns each incident into a change.

Risks are scored on likelihood and impact, each on a three-point scale. Likelihood reflects the platform's actual exposure — a single application host, one replica set, a small team — not a hypothetical adversary. Impact reflects the business consequence: whether the laundry can trade, whether records are lost, and whether obligations to clients are breached.

Table 55 — Scoring scales
ScoreLikelihoodImpact
HighExpected within a year on current controlsTrading stops, or data is lost or exposed
MediumPossible within one to three yearsA function is unavailable for hours, or figures are unreliable
LowUnlikely without a change in circumstancesLocal inconvenience, recoverable within a shift

9.2 Risk register

9 · Disaster ManagementLoveLaundry — System Manual

The register is reviewed quarterly and after every Severity 1 or 2 incident. Likelihood and impact are re-scored then; an entry that has not changed for a year is either genuinely stable or not being examined.

Table 56 — Risk register
RiskLikelihoodImpactMitigationOwner
Database corruption or lossLowHighNightly logical backups, oplog retention, quarterly restore drillsPlatform operator
Staff credential compromiseMediumHighShort token lifetime, capability checks, sign-in auditing, rapid disable and key rotationLaundry administrator
Ransomware on the application hostLowHighImmutable off-host backups, least-privilege accounts, no interactive browsing on the hostPlatform operator
Insider misuse of discounts or voidsMediumMediumReason codes, supervisor approval, reprint detection, day-close reconciliationLaundry owner
Cloud region outageLowHighDocumented rebuild in a second region, configuration held outside the region, DNS switchPlatform operator
Payment or messaging supplier outageMediumMediumManual fallback recorded in the day book, reconciliation on recoveryLaundry manager
Disk exhaustion on the database hostMediumHighCapacity alerts, log rotation, backup pruning, retention policyPlatform operator
Key loss (KEK or signing key)LowHighEscrowed KEK, documented rotation, staged key overlapPlatform operator
Silent billing error after a releaseMediumHighSuite gates, no Friday deploys, day-close review of unbilled itemsDeveloper
Note

The last entry is the one most often missed. A release that produces subtly wrong bills is worse than an outage, because nobody notices until clients do.

9.3 · Threat scenarios

Threat scenario — database loss

Scenario. The operations database is lost or corrupted: a failed migration, an accidental drop, or storage failure on the primary. Sign-in still works, because user_db is intact, which makes the incident look smaller than it is — staff can reach a dashboard that shows nothing.

Immediate signs

  • Every list view returns empty or errors while sign-in succeeds.
  • Service logs show connection failures or authentication errors against the operations database.
  • The MongoDB primary is unavailable and no election completes.

First actions

◆87◆
9 · Disaster ManagementLoveLaundry — System Manual
  1. Stop writes. Take bill_service out of the proxy rotation so that no partial records are created against a broken store.
  2. Confirm the scope: is the database unreachable, corrupted, or empty? These have different recovery paths.
  3. Check the replica set state and the most recent successful backup timestamp before attempting any repair.
  4. Declare severity: database loss affecting trading is Severity 1, and the response clock starts now.
  5. Begin the restore procedure in 10.4 in the fixed order: user_db, operations, accounting.
  6. Notify the laundry's manager with a factual statement and an expected next update time, not an estimate of recovery.

What not to do

Do not run a repair against the only copy. Do not restore over a database that might still be recoverable in place. Do not restart every service at once — the restart destroys the evidence in memory and makes the timeline harder to reconstruct. And do not accept a restored database without the verification steps in 10.5; a restore that loses yesterday's bills is a second incident.

Warning

If the loss is caused by a delete or a bad migration, point-in-time recovery (10.6) is almost always better than restoring last night's backup. Restore the backup only when the oplog cannot cover the window.

9.3 · Threat scenarios (continued)

Threat scenario — credential compromise

Scenario. A staff password is phished, or a token is copied from a shared terminal. Because tokens are stateless, the attacker can act as that user until the token expires — up to 24 hours — and every action will be attributed to the real person.

Detection

  • Sign-ins from unfamiliar addresses or at unusual hours, visible in the authentication log.
  • A burst of record creation or payment posting by one account.
  • A user reporting that they were signed out unexpectedly, or that records exist they did not create.

Containment

◆88◆
9 · Disaster ManagementLoveLaundry — System Manual
  1. Disable the affected user immediately. This prevents new tokens even though it does not revoke the existing one.
  2. Identify the capability of the compromised account: a STAFF token can create passes; an ADMIN token can change users.
  3. If the account held ADMIN or the token may have reached a privileged surface, rotate the signing key to invalidate every session (3.6).
  4. Preserve logs and audit entries before rotating, so the attacker's actions remain reconstructible.
  5. Review the account's actions during the exposure window and reverse anything fraudulent through the normal correction paths — never by editing records directly.
  6. Notify affected clients if their data was accessed, following 9.6.

Afterwards

Force a password reset for the user, review whether the password was reused elsewhere, and check whether the compromise came from a shared terminal. The most common root cause is not a sophisticated attack but a password written beside a counter terminal, and the control that fixes it is a lock screen and individual accounts.

Warning

Do not simply change the user's password. The existing token remains valid until expiry; disabling the account or rotating the key is the only way to stop it.

9.3 · Threat scenarios (continued)

Threat scenario — ransomware and insider misuse

Ransomware on the application host

Scenario. The host is encrypted by ransomware, either through a compromised remote-access account or through a downloaded file. The application stops; the database may be on the same host or reachable from it.

  1. Isolate the host from the network immediately. Do not shut it down if evidence may be needed, but do isolate it.
  2. Confirm that off-host backups exist and are immutable. This is the moment the design decision in 10.1 proves itself.
  3. Do not pay, and do not attempt decryption on the production host.
  4. Build a clean host from the documented deployment steps (8.5), then restore data (10.4).
  5. Rotate every credential the host could read: database users, storage keys, signing keys, KEK if it was present on the host.
  6. Report the incident, including any personal data exposure, per 9.6.

Insider misuse

Scenario. A member of staff issues refunds to themselves, voids bills after taking cash, applies discounts for friends, or exports client data. The pattern is usually small and repeated rather than large and obvious.

◆89◆
9 · Disaster ManagementLoveLaundry — System Manual
  • Prevention: reason codes, supervisor approval for refunds and discounts, capability separation between counter staff and managers, and no shared logins.
  • Detection: review refund and void frequency per user, compare discounts against the standard, and reconcile the drawer daily rather than monthly.
  • Response: preserve the audit records, involve the owner before confronting anyone, and correct the financial records through adjustment documents so that the client's statement stays true.
Note

Audit records are append-only and are the reason insider misuse is provable at all. Any proposal to allow editing or deleting audit entries should be refused on these grounds alone.

9.3 · Threat scenarios (continued)

Threat scenario — region outage and supplier outage

Cloud region outage

Scenario. The region hosting the application and database becomes unavailable: a provider incident, a network partition, or a sustained control-plane failure. Both the application and its primary database are unreachable, and the provider's own console may be degraded too.

  1. Confirm the outage is the provider's, not yours: check status pages from outside the region and test connectivity from a second location.
  2. Declare Severity 2 (or 1 if trading is impossible during business hours) and start the communication plan in 9.7.
  3. Do not attempt to rebuild in a second region until the provider confirms the primary region's state; a split-brain restore is worse than an outage.
  4. When confirmed unrecoverable within the business window, provision the second region from the documented steps, restore the latest off-host backup, and repoint DNS.
  5. Accept and record the data loss window: work recorded after the last backup but before the outage cannot be reconstructed from the platform and must be recovered from paper.

Supplier outage

Scenario. A payment terminal, SMS provider or email provider fails. The platform is healthy but one step of the business cannot complete.

Table 57 — Supplier failure fallbacks
SupplierImpactFallback
Card terminalCard payments cannot be takenRecord cash only, or record the card sale manually and reconcile when the terminal returns
SMS or emailClients do not receive notificationsPhone the client; the record is unaffected
Object storageBackups fail; document downloads may failKeep the local backup copy, alert immediately, and restore the storage path before the next scheduled backup
◆90◆
9 · Disaster ManagementLoveLaundry — System Manual
Note

A supplier outage is not a reason to bypass a control. Recording a card payment as cash to “keep moving” corrupts the day-close reconciliation and takes longer to unwind than the original outage.

9.4 · Incident severity matrix

Incident severity matrix

Severity determines who is called, how fast, and what is communicated. It is assigned at declaration and may be raised once, never lowered during the incident — a lower severity mid-incident invites people to stand down too early.

Table 58 — Severity levels, examples and targets
SeverityDefinitionExamplesResponse target
SEV1Trading impossible, data loss or exposureDatabase lost; sign-in broken for all; ransomwareAcknowledge 15 min, contain 1 h, update every 30 min
SEV2A major function unavailable, workaround existsHotel portal down; billing blocked for one client; region degradedAcknowledge 30 min, mitigate 4 h, update hourly
SEV3A minor function degraded, business continuesOne report failing; tag printing slow; single user blockedAcknowledge 4 h, resolve 2 business days
SEV4Cosmetic or single-user inconvenienceLabel misaligned; a filter not rememberedNext planned release

Who decides

The first responder declares the severity using this table, and the platform operator confirms or raises it. When in doubt, declare higher: the cost of an unnecessary SEV1 is a wasted hour, and the cost of a late SEV1 is a day of unbilled work.

Escalation

SEV1 involves the platform operator, the laundry owner and — where personal data may be involved — the person responsible for data protection. SEV2 involves the operator and the laundry manager. SEV3 and SEV4 are handled by the operator alone and reported in the weekly summary.

Warning

Severity is about business impact, not about how interesting the technical cause is. A dull configuration error that stops billing is SEV1; an exotic bug in a report nobody uses is SEV3.

9.5 · Response runbook

Response runbook

The runbook is written to be followed in the first hour, when information is incomplete and everyone is busy. Times are targets measured from declaration, not aspirations.

◆91◆
9 · Disaster ManagementLoveLaundry — System Manual
  1. T+0 — Declare. Name the incident, assign a severity, open a timeline document with the time and the reporter. One person owns the timeline.
  2. T+5 min — Stop the harm. Isolate the affected component: remove a service from rotation, disable an account, block an address. Containment before diagnosis.
  3. T+10 min — Assess data. Determine whether data is lost, exposed, or merely unavailable. This single question sets the recovery path and the notification obligation.
  4. T+15 min — Notify. SEV1: operator and owner by phone. SEV2: operator, then manager. State facts and the next update time; do not estimate recovery.
  5. T+30 min — Stabilise. Restore service from backup, fail over, or apply the documented workaround. Record every command that changes state.
  6. T+60 min — Verify. Run the smoke checks: sign-in, dashboard, one gate pass, one bill, one hotel portal read. Confirm with a real user, not only with a health endpoint.
  7. T+4 h — Reconcile. Identify work performed on paper during the outage, enter it with the correct dates, and note the delay in the record.
  8. T+24 h — Review. Hold the post-incident review within one business day, while memory is fresh; publish actions with owners and dates.
Note

The scribe is the most valuable role in a long incident and the first one omitted. A timeline written during the event is worth more than a reconstruction afterwards.

9.6 · Communication and review

Communication plan and post-incident review

9.6 Communication plan

◆92◆
9 · Disaster ManagementLoveLaundry — System Manual
Table 59 — Who is told what, and when
AudienceTriggerChannel and content
Laundry ownerSEV1, SEV2Phone within 15 minutes: what is affected, what is being done, next update time
Laundry manager and supervisorsAny severity affecting tradingDirect message: workaround instructions and what to record on paper
Hotel clientsTheir records or invoices are affectedWritten notice from the laundry: what happened, what was corrected, what they should check
All staffSEV1, or any change to procedureNotice at next sign-in or shift briefing
Data protection contactPersonal data may have been accessedImmediate written notice with the facts known at the time

Communication during an incident is factual and time-bound. Say what is known, what is not known, and when the next update will come. Never speculate about cause or recovery time, and never blame a named individual — the review establishes cause, not the incident channel.

9.7 Post-incident review

Every SEV1 and SEV2 incident gets a written review within one business day. The review is blameless in method but specific in outcome: it must produce changes with owners and dates, not a narrative of what everyone did wrong.

Table 60 — Review agenda
SectionContent
TimelineDetection, declaration, containment, recovery, verification — with times
ImpactWhat was unavailable, for how long, and which records were affected
CauseThe technical cause and the contributing conditions that let it matter
What workedControls that did their job, so they are not removed in the next redesign
ActionsSpecific changes, each with an owner and a due date
VerificationHow the fix will be tested, and when the review is closed
Warning

An action without an owner and a date is a wish. If a review produces more than five actions, it has produced none that will be done — choose the ones that change the outcome.

9.8 · Incident severity matrix

Incident severity matrix

One table that decides who is called and how fast.

◆93◆
9 · Disaster ManagementLoveLaundry — System Manual

Severity is assigned at declaration, from business impact rather than technical curiosity. A dull configuration error that stops billing is Sev1; an exotic defect in a report nobody reads is Sev3.

The matrix is read downwards, not upwards: start at the impact, then take the response target that belongs to it. The target is measured from declaration, not from the moment someone understands the cause.

Rule

Severity may be raised during an incident and is never lowered. Lowering it mid-incident invites people to stand down before the work is finished.

◆94◆
10

Part Three · Backup and Recovery

Backup and Recovery

◆

What is protected, how quickly it must come back, and how the restore is proved rather than assumed.

10.1 What is backed up

Backups exist to restore a business, not to archive a server. The inventory below therefore follows the three-database model: everything that cannot be rebuilt from source is backed up, and everything that can be rebuilt is not.

10 · Backup and RecoveryLoveLaundry — System Manual
Table 61 — Backup inventory
ItemMethodWhy it is backed up
user_dbNightly logical dump plus continuous oplogIdentity and tenancy; without it nobody can sign in
Operations databaseNightly logical dump plus continuous oplogGate passes, deliveries, bills, linen history — the trading record
Accounting databaseNightly logical dumpLedger and payroll; changes slowly, restored independently
Uploaded documents and printed artefactsObject-storage versioningBill PDFs and attachments referenced by records
ConfigurationVersion-controlled environment templates, secrets in the key storeA host can be rebuilt only if its configuration is known
KEK and search-key escrowSeparate secure escrow, distinct access policyEncrypted fields are unreadable without them
Audit logAppend-only log pipeline with extended retentionNeeded for investigation after an incident

What is deliberately not backed up

Front-end bundles are rebuilt from the tagged commit, not backed up as files. Container images are rebuilt from the same commit. Temporary caches, session state and search indexes hold nothing that cannot be reconstructed. Backing these up would lengthen every restore without changing the outcome.

Warning

A backup that has never been restored is a hypothesis. The drill in 10.7 exists because the most common backup failure is a backup that completes successfully and cannot be read.

10.2 · RPO and RTO targets

Recovery objectives

Recovery point objective (RPO) is how much data the business can afford to lose. Recovery time objective (RTO) is how long it can afford to be without the function. Both are business statements that the technical design must meet — not measurements of what happens to be possible.

Table 62 — Targets per component
ComponentRPORTOBasis
user_db15 minutes1 hourOplog replay from the last dump; identity is a precondition for everything
Operations database15 minutes2 hoursOplog replay; the trading record, largest restore
Accounting database24 hours4 hoursDaily dump is sufficient; restores independently
Object storage24 hours1 hourVersioning; documents referenced by records
Application hostNot applicable2 hoursRebuilt from configuration, no state
Full estate15 minutes4 hoursSequential restore in dependency order
◆96◆
10 · Backup and RecoveryLoveLaundry — System Manual
Note

The 15-minute RPO depends on the oplog being intact. If the oplog is lost with the database, the achievable RPO becomes 24 hours, which is why the oplog is replicated off-host and monitored as a first-class backup artefact.

10.3 · Backup schedule

Backup schedule

Backups run on a schedule, are copied off-host, and are verified by a job that reads them back. A backup job that reports success without a verification step is reporting that a file was written, not that it can be used.

Table 63 — Schedule and retention
JobFrequencyRetentionDestination
user_db logical dumpDaily 01:0035 daily, 12 monthlyObject storage, separate account
Operations dumpDaily 01:1535 daily, 12 monthlyObject storage, separate account
Accounting dumpDaily 01:3035 daily, 24 monthlyObject storage, separate account
Oplog archiveContinuous72 hoursObject storage, separate account
Configuration snapshotOn every deploymentIndefinite (version control)Repository
Restore verificationWeeklyLatest verified copy recordedIsolated environment
Full drillQuarterlyReport retained 2 yearsIsolated environment

Ordering and overlap

The three dumps are staggered so that they do not compete for disk or network, and so that a failure in one does not delay the others. The operations dump is the longest and runs second; the accounting dump is small and runs last. Every job writes a manifest containing the start time, end time, byte count, database name and checksum, which is what the verification job reads.

Monitoring the schedule

◆97◆
10 · Backup and RecoveryLoveLaundry — System Manual
  • A missed job raises an alert within 15 minutes of its expected completion.
  • A job that completes with a size more than 20 percent below its recent average is treated as suspect and alerted, not accepted.
  • Two consecutive verification failures are a Severity 2 incident, because the business is one failure away from having no usable backup.
Warning

Never store the only backup copy on the host being backed up. Ransomware and disk failure both remove the backup and the data in one event.

10.4 · Restore procedure

Restore procedure

Restore order is fixed: user_db first, operations second, accounting third. Operations documents reference users and memberships; accounting references operational documents. Restoring out of order produces a database that looks complete and is internally inconsistent.

Procedure — restoring to a clean host

  1. Freeze. Take the application out of service so that no writes occur during the restore. Announce the maintenance window.
  2. Provision. Build the host and install the database version recorded in the release notes. Do not restore into a different major version without a tested upgrade path.
  3. Fetch. Retrieve the chosen dump and its manifest from object storage. Verify the checksum against the manifest before use.
  4. Restore user_db. Load the dump, then apply oplog entries up to the target time if point-in-time recovery is required.
  5. Verify identity. Confirm that users, laundries and memberships are present and that a known administrator can authenticate.
  6. Restore operations. Load the dump into the operations database and replay the oplog to the same target time.
  7. Restore accounting. Load the accounting dump, then reconcile its payment totals against the restored operations data.
  8. Re-encrypt check. Confirm that a known encrypted field decrypts with the escrowed KEK. A restore with the wrong key is indistinguishable from data loss until someone opens a record.
  9. Start services. Bring services up in dependency order and run the smoke checks in 10.5.
  10. Record. Write the restore record: operator, dump identifiers, target time, duration, verification results.
Warning

Do not restore over a live database in place. Restore into a fresh database, verify, then switch the connection string. An in-place restore that fails halfway leaves neither the old data nor the new.

◆98◆
10 · Backup and RecoveryLoveLaundry — System Manual

10.5 · Verification and integrity checks

Verification and integrity checks

A restore is complete when the data is proved usable, not when the load command exits. The checks below run in order; the first failure stops the process and the restore is repeated from the previous step.

Table 64 — Post-restore checks
CheckMethodPass condition
Row countsCount per collection against the manifestWithin the recorded tolerance; no empty core collection
IdentitySign in as a known administratorSign-in succeeds and the tenant resolves
TenancyRequest a record with a foreign tenant identifierReturns not-found, never a record
Financial continuitySum bill totals, payments and balancesBalances equal totals less payments; no negative balance without a credit record
Referential integrityDeliveries without a pass; bills without linesZero orphans
Linen consistencyTags in a status with no corresponding eventZero, or explained by the restore window
EncryptionOpen a record with an encrypted fieldDecrypts correctly; no key errors in the log
Recent activityOpen the last gate pass before the failurePresent with its deliveries intact

Integrity queries worth keeping

The financial check is the one that catches a partial restore most reliably, because a half-loaded set of payments still looks plausible in a list but cannot balance. The orphan check catches a restore that stopped between collections, which is exactly what happens when a restore is interrupted and resumed incorrectly.

// deliveries whose gate pass is absent
{"$lookup": {"from": "gate_passes", "localField": "gate_pass_id",
              "foreignField": "_id", "as": "gp"}},
{"$match": {"gp": []}}
Note

Keep the verification queries in version control alongside the restore script. A check that exists only in someone's memory is not a control.

10.6 · Point-in-time recovery

Point-in-time recovery

Point-in-time recovery (PITR) restores the database to a moment before a damaging change — a bad migration, a mistaken delete, a corrupting script. It combines the last full dump with oplog entries replayed up to, but not including, the harmful operation.

Procedure — recovering to a chosen moment

◆99◆
10 · Backup and RecoveryLoveLaundry — System Manual
  1. Identify the exact time of the harmful change from the audit log or the application log. Precision matters: replaying one minute too far re-applies the damage.
  2. Confirm that the required window is inside the oplog retention. Outside it, only a full restore is possible.
  3. Restore the most recent dump that precedes the target time into a fresh database.
  4. Replay oplog entries from the dump's end time to the target time, excluding the harmful operation.
  5. Verify with the checks in 10.5, then switch the connection string and restart the services.
  6. Reconcile any work performed after the target time from paper or from client records, and enter it with its true date and a note explaining the gap.
Table 65 — Choosing the recovery point
SituationTarget timeRationale
Accidental delete of one collectionJust before the deleteMinimises lost legitimate work
Bad migration altering many recordsJust before the migration startedThe migration's effects are the damage
Corruption of unknown originLast verified good statePrefer a known-good point to a guessed one
RansomwareLast backup before encryption beganAssume everything after is untrusted
Warning

Replaying to the exact second of a transaction boundary can leave a bill without its payment. Choose a recovery point at a quiet moment — end of day, or after a close — whenever the business can tolerate it.

10.7 · Restore drill checklist

Restore drill checklist

The drill is performed quarterly against an isolated environment, using the same artefacts and the same procedure as a real recovery. It is timed, and the result is recorded — including the parts that failed.

Table 66 — Drill checklist
StepCheckEvidence recorded
1Retrieve the latest dump and verify its checksumDump identifier, checksum, retrieval time
2Provision an isolated host with the recorded versionsHost identifier, versions
3Restore user_db and authenticate as a known administratorTime to first successful sign-in
4Restore operations and accounting databasesTime per database, total elapsed
5Run the integrity checks in 10.5Each check's result, including failures
6Decrypt a known sensitive field with the escrowed KEKField identifier, result
7Replay a five-minute oplog windowTarget time, entries applied
8Run the smoke tests: pass, delivery, bill, hotel readScreenshots or ids of created records
9Compare achieved RPO and RTO with the targetsMeasured values against 10.2
10Destroy the isolated environmentDestruction time, operator
◆100◆
10 · Backup and RecoveryLoveLaundry — System Manual

What the drill must produce

  • A measured restore duration, compared with the RTO. A drill that is not timed does not test the objective.
  • A list of every step that required improvisation, because each is a gap in this chapter.
  • Confirmation that the KEK escrow works from a clean environment, not from the operator's workstation.
  • An updated procedure if any step was wrong. The manual is corrected the same week, not at the next review.
Note

Record failures in the drill report. A clean report that everyone knows was helped along is worse than a failed drill that gets fixed.

10.8 · Backup and recovery timeline

Backup and recovery timeline

Three overlapping protections, and the fifteen minutes that separates them.

The restore procedure itself begins on page 98, and the drill checklist on page 100. The timeline explains why the recovery-point target is fifteen minutes rather than a day. The nightly dump sets the floor, the oplog closes the gap to the moment of failure, and the off-host copy survives the loss of the host that wrote it.

Each layer answers a different failure. The dump answers corruption, the oplog answers a bad change made an hour ago, and the off-host copy answers the loss of the account in which everything else lives.

Rule

The oplog is a backup artefact, not a log to be pruned for space. If it is lost with the database, the achievable recovery point becomes the last dump.

◆101◆
11

Part Three · Fail-Safes and Resilience

Fail-Safes and Resilience

◆

How the platform behaves when something is missing, slow, or called twice.

11.1 Fail-closed tenancy

The platform's most important fail-safe is also its simplest: when the tenant cannot be established, nothing happens. There is no default tenant, no fallback to an unscoped query, and no “system” mode that skips the check. A request that cannot name its laundry is refused before it reaches any data.

Table 67 — Failure conditions and outcomes
ConditionOutcomeWhy
No token401Identity is unknown
Expired or badly signed token401Identity cannot be trusted
Client token on a staff route403No tenant claim exists to resolve
Staff token with no laundry_id403Tenant context missing; fail closed
Membership removed since issue403 after the account is disabledCapabilities are snapshot at sign-in
Foreign identifier in a path404Indistinguishable from a non-existent record

Why fail closed rather than fail open

11 · Fail-Safes and ResilienceLoveLaundry — System Manual

A fail-open design answers a missing tenant with “all tenants”, which turns a configuration mistake into a data breach. Fail-closed turns the same mistake into an outage — visible, recoverable, and confined to the person who caused it. For a multi-tenant system holding other businesses' commercial records, an outage is the cheaper failure every time.

Note

The same principle applies to capabilities: an unknown or missing capability is treated as absent, never as permitted. New routes must declare a capability or they cannot be reached at all.

11.2 · Idempotency and concurrency

Idempotency and optimistic concurrency

Two failures cause most duplicate records in operational systems: a retried request that actually succeeded, and two users editing the same document. The platform addresses both explicitly rather than hoping they are rare.

Idempotency keys

Every write that creates money or possession — bill, payment, delivery, gate pass — accepts an idempotency key generated by the client. The server records the key with the result. A retry with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a second record, whether the first attempt succeeded, failed, or is still in progress.

Optimistic concurrency

Documents that can be edited carry a version. An update must state the version it read; if the stored version has moved, the write is rejected with a conflict instead of silently overwriting a colleague's change. The user is shown both versions and chooses — which is slower by one interaction and correct by construction.

Table 68 — Concurrency outcomes
SituationResponseUser experience
Same document, sequential editsAccepted; version incrementsNormal editing
Same document, simultaneous editsSecond write rejected with 409Message shows the other change; reload and retry
Retry after timeoutIdempotency key returns the original resultThe action appears to have succeeded, because it did
Duplicate key without a stored resultWrite rejected as in-progressThe user is asked to wait rather than double-submit
◆103◆
11 · Fail-Safes and ResilienceLoveLaundry — System Manual
Note

Idempotency keys are generated per form submission, not per user action. Reopening a bill and paying again is a new intent and gets a new key, which is why the confirmation step matters.

11.3 · Atomic bill and payment transitions

Atomic bill and payment transitions

Money movements are the one place where a partial write is unacceptable. A payment that reduces a balance without being recorded, or a bill that is issued without its lines, is worse than a failed request because it is invisible until reconciliation.

What must happen together

Table 69 — Atomic units
OperationWrites that must commit together
Issue billBill document with lines and totals; sequence number; client balance
Post paymentPayment record; bill balance; receipt reference; audit entry
Reverse paymentReversal record referencing the original; restored balance; audit entry
Record deliveryDelivery document; pass line delivered quantities; pass status
Close dayDay-close record with totals; frozen date marker; audit entry

MongoDB multi-document transactions make each of these a single unit. The platform uses them only where the invariant spans documents — a transaction has a cost, and paying it on a read is waste. Where a single document holds the whole invariant, an atomic update on that document is sufficient and cheaper.

Why the bill is not edited after issue

An issued bill is a document the client may already hold. Editing it would change the meaning of a record that exists outside the platform, and no transaction can undo that. Corrections are therefore new documents — credit notes, adjustments, reversals — each referencing the original, so the history remains a sequence of facts rather than a current opinion.

Warning

Never “fix” a balance by writing the field directly. A balance is derived from records; writing it creates a number that no document supports, and the next reconciliation will fail with no explanation.

11.4 · Offline cache, retries and circuit breaking

Offline cache, retries and circuit breaking

A laundry is a physical place with unreliable connectivity: a basement linen room, a counter by a steel door, a driver's phone. The front ends are built to stay useful for reading when the network is poor, and to refuse to pretend when it is absent.

Offline cache behaviour

◆104◆
11 · Fail-Safes and ResilienceLoveLaundry — System Manual
  • Cached reads, never cached writes. Lists and detail views may be served from the last successful response, clearly marked as cached with the time it was fetched.
  • No queued writes. The platform does not store a write locally and replay it later with an invented timestamp. A scan recorded at 14:05 must not enter the system as 09:12.
  • Explicit staleness. A cached view says when it was last updated; a user who sees “as of 09:12” knows to phone rather than assume.
  • Sign-out clears the cache. Cached business data does not survive a session on a shared terminal.

Retries and queues

Reads retry automatically with exponential backoff and jitter, up to a small limit. Writes retry only when the request is idempotent, and always with the same key, so that a retry cannot create a second bill. Where a write triggers a cross-service side effect — mirroring a payment into accounting — the platform writes a durable outbox record in the same transaction as the business write and processes it asynchronously. If the accounting service is down, the payment still posts; the outbox retries until it succeeds, and the discrepancy is visible rather than lost.

Circuit breaking

When a dependency fails repeatedly, the caller stops calling it for a short period and fails fast instead of queueing requests that will time out. This protects the healthy services from thread and connection exhaustion caused by one sick dependency. The breaker closes automatically after a successful probe, and its state is exposed as a health detail so that an operator can see “degraded because accounting is down” rather than a generic error.

Note

Fail fast is a feature. A request that waits thirty seconds and then fails is worse for the user and for the system than one that fails in fifty milliseconds and says why.

11.5 · Degraded-mode matrix

Degraded-mode matrix

The matrix states what still works when a component is unavailable. It is written from the operator's point of view: during an incident, the question is never “which service is down?” but “can we still take in laundry and bill for it?”

◆105◆
11 · Fail-Safes and ResilienceLoveLaundry — System Manual
Table 70 — Capability by failed component
If this is down…Still worksStopsWorkaround
user-serviceNothing authenticatedEverythingRestore identity first — it is the precondition for all else
bill_serviceSign-in; quotations; accounting readsPasses, deliveries, bills, linen, shop, hotel portalPaper records with times; enter after recovery
laundry-managementAll operational workAccounting posting, payroll, expense entryOutbox queues payments; reconcile after recovery
quotation-serviceAll operational and financial workQuotation drafting and AI chatPrice manually and record once service returns
worker-serviceAll operational workWorker lists and attendanceRecord attendance on paper for the shift
MongoDB primaryReads served by secondary, brieflyAll writesWait for election; do not force a primary

Reverse proxyNothing from outsideAll client accessRestore proxy config; services remain healthy

Reading the matrix in an incident

The first column that is empty tells you the severity. If sign-in is down, everything is down and the incident is SEV1 regardless of the technical cause. If only accounting is down, the laundry can trade all day and the incident is SEV2 with an outbox reconciliation afterwards.

Warning

A workaround that bypasses a control is not a workaround. Paper records are acceptable; entering a bill twice “to be safe”, or marking a card payment as cash, is not.

11.6 · Guard rails against double billing

Guard rails against double billing

Double billing is the failure clients notice fastest and forgive slowest. The platform defends against it at four layers, so that no single mistake — human or technical — can produce a duplicate charge.

Table 71 — Four layers of defence
LayerControlWhat it prevents
DataA delivery line can belong to only one billThe same delivered quantity being billed twice
TransactionBill issue and delivery marking commit togetherA bill issued without consuming its deliveries
RequestIdempotency key on bill creationA retried issue creating a second bill
ProcessDay-close review of unbilled deliveries and duplicate totalsAnything the first three layers missed
◆106◆
11 · Fail-Safes and ResilienceLoveLaundry — System Manual

How a duplicate would still be caught

  1. The bill list shows consecutive bills for the same client with identical totals and periods — flagged in the day-close review.
  2. A delivery already consumed by a bill is not offered when raising the next bill, so the second attempt produces an empty selection rather than a duplicate.
  3. A client statement shows both invoices with their numbers; the hotel portal makes the duplicate visible to the client the same day.
  4. The audit trail records who issued each bill and when, which distinguishes a duplicate from a legitimate re-issue.

Correcting a duplicate

Void the duplicate with a reason and re-check the client's balance. Do not delete it: a voided bill keeps its number and remains visible, which is what allows the client's copy and the platform's record to agree. If the duplicate has been paid, reverse the payment and void the bill, then issue a credit note if the client's money must be returned through accounting.

Note

Every guard rail here is also a test in the bill_service suite. The controls and the tests are maintained together, because a guard rail that is not tested is a comment.

11.7 · Guard layers against double billing

Guard layers against double billing

Four independent defences, so that no single mistake produces a duplicate charge.

◆107◆
11 · Fail-Safes and ResilienceLoveLaundry — System Manual

A duplicate charge is the failure clients notice fastest and forgive slowest, so the platform does not rely on one control. The data model prevents a delivered line from belonging to two bills; the transaction prevents a bill from existing without consuming its lines; the idempotency key prevents a retry from creating a second document.

The fourth layer is human and deliberately boring: the day-close review looks for consecutive bills with identical totals. It exists to catch the combinations the first three layers cannot foresee.

Rule

Each layer is also a test in the bill_service suite. A control that is not asserted is a comment, and comments do not survive refactoring.

Part Four · Testing and Quality Assurance

Testing and Quality Assurance

◆

What is tested, what the suites actually report, and what remains unproven.

12.1 Test strategy

The strategy is a pyramid, and it is deliberately bottom-heavy. Most behaviour is verified by fast service-level tests that exercise real handlers against a test database; a smaller number of integration tests cover cross-service contracts; and the top of the pyramid — where confidence is most expensive — is thin. That is a deliberate trade: a browser-driven suite for four applications would be slow, brittle, and rarely run.

12 · Testing and Quality AssuranceLoveLaundry — System Manual

LayerExercisesRuns in
UnitPure functions: totals, tax, status transitions, token parsingSeconds, no database
ServiceHTTP handlers with authentication and a test databaseThe service's own suite
IntegrationCross-service flows: login → pass → delivery → bill; client portal scopebill_service and user-service suites
BuildTypeScript compilation and Vite production build for all four appsCI or local release check
ManualExploratory checks of new screens and print layoutsBefore each release
Note

Tests run against a real MongoDB instance, not a mock. Tenancy and transaction behaviour are precisely the things a mock cannot reproduce, and they are the properties most worth testing.

Measured results

The figures below are measured from the suites as they stand. They are reported as counts of passing tests, not as coverage percentages, because a coverage number would say more about the size of the codebase than about whether the important behaviour is verified.

How to read these numbers

A passing suite means the behaviour it asserts still holds. It does not mean the product is defect-free, and the two skipped tests are skipped deliberately rather than hidden: they cover paths that require an external dependency not configured in the current environment. Chapter 12.3 states the gaps plainly.

What is deliberately not claimed

  • No coverage percentage is quoted, because line coverage would be misleading for a codebase with a large amount of declarative schema.
  • No performance figures are quoted, because no load test has been run.
  • No browser-level pass rate is quoted, because there is no browser-driven end-to-end suite.
Note

Reporting a measured 380 rather than a rounded “over 400” is itself part of the quality claim. The manual should not be more confident than the suites.

12.4 · Running the suites

Running the suites

Each service has its own virtual environment and its own suite. Running them is a local operation and requires a reachable MongoDB instance; the tests create and drop their own database.

Service suites

cd shop-app
npm ci

# repeat for hotel-app, linen-room-app, quotations-ui

A successful build is the release gate for the front ends: TypeScript must compile with no errors and Vite must emit a bundle. Warnings are reviewed but do not block a release unless they indicate an unused secret or a missing environment variable.

Why these are stated rather than hidden

A manual that lists only what works is a sales document. The value of this chapter is that a new maintainer can see exactly where confidence ends — and can decide, with the owner, whether a gap matters for the next release. The gaps above are known, bounded and owned; none of them is a surprise waiting to be discovered during an incident.

Closing the httpx2 gap requires only adding the dependency to the test requirements. It is listed as a limitation rather than fixed here because this manual reports the environment as measured, not as it could be.

Part Four · Operations Runbook and Monitoring

Operations Runbook and Monitoring

◆

The routine that keeps the platform observable, and the first five minutes of the incidents that interrupt it.

13.1 Health checks

Each service exposes a health endpoint that answers two questions separately: is the process alive, and can it reach what it depends on? A single combined check is worse than useless, because it cannot distinguish a dead service from a healthy service with a dead database.

Table 77 — Health probes
ProbeChecksUsed by
LivenessProcess responds; no dependency accessSupervisor restart policy
ReadinessDatabase reachable; key material loadedReverse proxy rotation
Deep healthDatabase round-trip, key version, outbox backlogMonitoring, every minute
Auth probeA known test account can sign in (staging only)Release verification
13 · Operations Runbook and MonitoringLoveLaundry — System Manual

Health output is JSON with a status per dependency, so that a monitoring system can alert on the specific dependency rather than on “service unhealthy”. The outbox backlog is included because a service that is healthy but cannot drain its queue is failing slowly and silently.

Note

Never use a deep health check as a liveness probe. A database blip would then restart healthy services, turning a short dependency failure into a restart storm.

13.2 · Logs

Logs

Logs are structured JSON, one event per line, written to stdout and collected by the log pipeline. They are designed to answer “who did what, to which record, in which tenant, and did it work?” without a debugger.

Table 78 — Log fields
FieldContent
timeISO-8601 timestamp with offset
levelinfo, warning, error
serviceuser-service, bill_service, and so on
request_idCorrelates every log line from one request, including cross-service calls
user_id / roleActor, when authenticated
laundry_idTenant, when resolved — never a tenant guessed from the payload
actionRoute or operation name
targetRecord identifier, when applicable
outcomeStatus code or result class
duration_msHandler duration

What is never logged

  • Passwords, in any form, including on failed sign-in.
  • Bearer tokens or signing keys.
  • Full request bodies for authentication and payment routes.
  • Personal data beyond what an audit entry requires.
◆116◆
13 · Operations Runbook and MonitoringLoveLaundry — System Manual

Retention and access

Application logs are retained for 30 days at full detail and 12 months at reduced detail. Audit entries are retained for seven years and are append-only. Access to logs is restricted to the platform operator; a laundry administrator may be given a filtered extract for their own tenant when investigating a dispute, but never a cross-tenant view.

Warning

A stack trace that includes a connection string is a credential leak. The logging configuration redacts known secret patterns, but new code must not log configuration objects wholesale.

13.3 · Alerts and first response

Alerts and first response

An alert is only useful if the first action is obvious. Each alert below names the likely cause and the first thing to check, so that the person woken at night does not begin with an investigation.

Table 79 — Alert catalogue
AlertLikely causeFirst response
Sign-in failure rate above baselineCredential stuffing, or a broken key rotationCheck the failure reason distribution; block the source if it is external
5xx rate above baseline on bill_serviceDatabase unreachable, or a bad releaseCheck readiness and the most recent deployment
Backup job missedScheduler stopped, or storage credential expiredRun the job manually; verify the credential
Backup size drop > 20%Partial dump or empty databaseTreat as failed; do not rotate retention until explained
Disk usage above 80%Log growth or oplog retentionPrune logs, verify retention policy, plan capacity
Oplog window below 24 hoursWrite volume outpacing oplog sizeIncrease oplog size before the RPO degrades
Outbox backlog growingAccounting service unavailableCheck the dependency; the queue drains on recovery
Certificate expiring in 14 daysRenewal failedRenew manually; verify the proxy reload
Repeated 403 on one accountRole removed, or a client token used on a staff routeConfirm the account type and membership

Escalation discipline

Acknowledge, then act. An alert acknowledged and forgotten is worse than one ignored, because it hides the problem from everyone else. If the first response does not resolve the alert within its target, escalate the severity rather than extending the window quietly.

Note

Alert fatigue is a design defect. If an alert fires routinely without action, either the threshold is wrong or the underlying problem should be fixed; leaving it in place trains people to ignore the one that matters.

◆117◆
13 · Operations Runbook and MonitoringLoveLaundry — System Manual

13.4 · Routine maintenance calendar

Routine maintenance calendar

Maintenance is scheduled so that it never competes with a day close or a Monday collection. The calendar is deliberately boring: the same tasks, at the same cadence, with the same owner.

Table 80 — Maintenance schedule
CadenceTaskOwner
DailyVerify the overnight backups completed and their sizes are normalPlatform operator
DailyReview the error log for new patternsPlatform operator
WeeklyRun the restore verification job against the latest dumpPlatform operator
WeeklyReview refunds, voids and discounts by userLaundry manager
MonthlyApply operating-system and dependency security updatesPlatform operator
MonthlyReview disk, oplog window and database growthPlatform operator
QuarterlyFull restore drill with timing (10.7)Platform operator
QuarterlyReview the risk register and incident actionsOwner and operator
AnnuallyRotate the search key with a planned backfillPlatform operator
AnnuallyReview roles, memberships and dormant accountsLaundry administrator
Warning

Never apply security updates to the database host during trading hours without a tested rollback. A patched database that will not start is an outage with a maintenance window's worth of warning wasted.

13.5 · Alert and escalation flow

Alert and escalation flow

From signal to review, with the loop that raises severity when nobody answers.

◆118◆
13 · Operations Runbook and MonitoringLoveLaundry — System Manual

An alert is only useful if the first action is obvious, so every alert in the catalogue names a likely cause and the first thing to check. The flow above is the path from a signal to a written action, and it is deliberately short.

The loop at the top is the part that is usually missing: if nobody acknowledges within the target, severity is raised rather than the window quietly extended.

Rule

An alert that fires routinely without action is a design defect. Either the threshold is wrong or the cause should be fixed; leaving it trains people to ignore the one that matters.

Appendix C

Status enumerations

Statuses are stored as fixed strings. They are listed here because they appear in exports, reports and hotel-facing documents, and parsed by external tools that must not invent new values.

◆124◆
AppendicesLoveLaundry — System Manual
Table 89 — Status values by document
DocumentValuesNotes
Gate passreceived, in_wash, ready, delivered, closed, cancelledCancelled passes retain their number
Deliveryrecorded, reversedReversal is a new record referencing the original
Billdraft, issued, part_paid, paid, voidIssued bills are immutable
Paymentposted, reversedReversal never deletes the original
Shop billdraft, open, paid, refunded, voidSeparate numbering from laundry bills
Quotationdraft, sent, accepted, declined, expiredConversion creates work, not a bill
Linen tagcollected, received, in_wash, washed, pressed, ready, delivered, missing, damaged, retiredTen lifecycle states, forward transitions only
Discrepancyopen, resolved, written_offResolution requires a supervisor
Client accountactive, disabledDisabled blocks new sign-ins
Useractive, disabledMembership removal is separate from disabling

Why fixed strings

Free-text statuses make reports unreliable, because every spelling becomes a category. Fixed enumerations mean the monthly matrix, the dashboard and the hotel portal all count the same thing. When a new status is genuinely required, it is added to the enumeration, to the transition rules and to the tests in the same change.

Warning

Never write a status that is not in this table. A value the platform does not recognise will disappear from every filtered view while remaining in the database, which is the hardest kind of missing record to find.

Appendix D

Glossary

Terms as they are used in this manual and in the interface. Where a term has a narrower meaning here than in general use, the narrower meaning applies.

◆125◆
AppendicesLoveLaundry — System Manual
Table 90 — Glossary of terms
TermDefinition
Audit entryAn append-only record of a security-relevant action: actor, tenant, action, target, outcome.
CapabilityA named permission such as bill:write, carried in the token and checked per route.
Client accountA hotel login stored in client_accounts; scoped to one laundry and one client_name.
client_nameThe string identifying a hotel on operational documents. Not an entity, not a tenant.
client_scopeThe claim object on a client token containing laundry_id and client_name.
Day closeThe act of freezing a business date's totals and recording who closed it.
DEKData encryption key: a per-document key used with AES-256-GCM.
DeliveryThe record of returning finished goods against a gate pass.
DiscrepancyA recorded mismatch in quantity, condition or status.
Gate passThe document recording goods received from a client and the promise to return them.
Idempotency keyA client-generated key that makes a retried write return the original result.
KEKKey-encryption key: wraps DEKs and is held outside the database.
MembershipThe link between a user and a laundry, carrying a role.
Monthly matrixA client-by-day grid of quantities and values derived from passes and deliveries.
OutboxA durable record of a side effect to be retried until it succeeds.
RPO / RTORecovery point objective (acceptable data loss) and recovery time objective (acceptable downtime).
Search tokenAn HMAC-SHA256 value enabling equality search over encrypted fields.
TenantA laundry; identified by laundry_id on every business document.
token_kindA claim distinguishing staff tokens from client tokens.

Maintenance of this manual

The manual is reviewed at every minor release and after every Severity 1 or 2 incident. A change to the platform that alters a procedure, an endpoint, a status value or a control requires a corresponding change here in the same release — a manual that lags the software is worse than no manual, because it is trusted.

Note

Corrections are recorded as new revisions rather than silent edits. The revision table is the record of what changed and when, and it is the first thing a new maintainer should read.
